body.heading: One more chair is a decision
paragraphs: Every family gathering has a natural size, and then there is the person just outside it: the neighbour who will be alone, the colleague new to the city, the friend whose own family is far away. Making room is rarely about space or food — there is almost always enough of both. It is about deciding that the circle is the kind that opens.
Ask early rather than at the last minute. An invitation given a week ahead says 'we thought of you'; one given on the day can feel like an afterthought, even when it is kindly meant.

body.heading: Brief your own side
paragraphs: Tell the regulars who is coming and one thing about them, so the newcomer is not met with a wall of shared references. Seat them beside your most hospitable talker, not your most impressive one. The goal is a guest who leaves feeling they were at a dinner, not an audition.
Children are often the best welcomers: a tour of the house, an explanation of the family's stranger customs, a place saved next to them. Give them the job formally and watch them take it seriously.

body.heading: It changes the table
paragraphs: A guest widens the conversation, brings new stories, and shows children that the family's warmth is not a closed system. Many permanent friendships — and a few permanent seats — begin with one extra chair.
Start with the lowest-stakes gathering you have, not the biggest holiday of the year. One successful extra chair makes the next one easier to imagine.

description: An early invitation, a briefed family, and a good seat: making room for one more person at a family gathering is a learnable kindness.
